## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-03.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical Overview – First Generation

No operating system yet – the open-shop era
Machine-code programming
Plugboards, later punched cards
Single-tasking operation
The programmer also operated the computer
Queuing for machine time

Problems: time-consuming, inefficient, no protection mechanisms

Plugboard (IBM 1401) – HubPages

Punched card
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-04.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical Overview – Second Generation

A dedicated operator ran the computer – closed-shop model
The operator collected programmers' punched cards
Their contents were copied to magnetic tape
Jobs were grouped into batches and executed (batch processing)
Output was written to magnetic tape and then printed
By the end of the era, a program took over the operator's role (Monitor, e.g. GM-NAA I/O)
Advantage: better resource utilization. 
Disadvantages: still single-tasking, long waiting times

Image source: Andrew S. Tanenbaum – Modern Operating Systems
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-05.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical Overview – Third Generation

The first operating systems appeared (OS/360)
Multiprogramming – multiple programs in memory
Spooling systems – I/O operations overlap with program execution
Time-sharing systems – CPU time was divided into slices; terminals appeared
Advantages: higher efficiency, user-friendly, interactive. 
Disadvantages: greater hardware requirements, more complex systems

Time-Sharing Operating System – GeeksforGeeks

Multiprogramming
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-06.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical Overview – Fourth Generation

Emergence of modern operating systems
Multitasking – one user running multiple programs
Multiuser – multiple users at the same time
Widespread use of network and real-time operating systems
Emergence of graphical user interfaces (GUI)
Security and protection – user isolation, permissions, access control
Virtual memory – secondary storage used as an extension of main memory

Advantages: usability, networking, standardization
Disadvantages: complexity, resource requirements, vulnerabilities
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-07.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Historical Overview – Fifth Generation

Today's operating systems
Parallel and distributed systems → clusters, grid computing, shared resource management across multiple computers.
Network and Internet integration → networking (e.g. TCP/IP) is a core part of the OS.
Mobile and embedded operating systems → Android, iOS, RTOS solutions.
Virtualization and containers → multiple virtual machines and containers on one physical system.
Security and access control → encryption, sandboxing, permission management.
Intelligent, self-adaptive operation → AI-based resource optimization, power management, predictive scheduling.
Cloud-oriented operating systems → designed for entire infrastructures rather than a single computer (e.g. container and VM management systems).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-08.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
What Is an Operating System?

An operating system is a collection of programs that manages computer resources and interacts with users.

Hardware provides the computer's physical resources (CPU, memory, secondary storage, network, peripherals).
The operating system controls and manages these resources and provides a secure, consistent environment for running programs.
Applications access hardware through the operating system, so they do not need to communicate directly with physical devices.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-09.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Typical Functions of Operating Systems

Process management and scheduling – controlling running programs and enabling multitasking.
Memory management – allocating memory to programs and protecting against invalid access.
File-system management – managing files and directories and providing access to them.
I/O device management – handling keyboards, monitors, printers, network adapters, etc.
User interface – providing a command-line or graphical environment.
Protection and security – access control and permission management.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-10.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Optional Functions of Operating Systems

Network services – communication protocols and network connectivity.
Virtual-machine and container management – isolated execution environments.
User and workgroup management – for example, on server systems.
Built-in applications and utilities – e.g. text editors and media players.
Power management – especially on mobile devices.
Special security features – encryption, firewall, antivirus protection.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-11.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Classification of Operating Systems – Classical Categories

Mainframe operating systems – run on mainframes and manage very large resources (e.g. IBM z/OS).
Server operating systems – provide network services to many clients (e.g. Windows Server, Linux server distributions).
Multiprocessor operating systems – run on multi-CPU or multicore systems and are optimized for parallel processing.
Personal-computer operating systems – desktop and laptop systems with user-friendly interfaces (e.g. Windows 11, macOS, desktop Linux).
Handheld-device operating systems – mobile phones, PDAs, tablets (e.g. Android, iOS).
Embedded operating systems – specialized hardware (e.g. cars, routers, IoT devices; often Linux variants or an RTOS).
Sensor-network operating systems – for small, resource-constrained sensors (e.g. TinyOS, Contiki).
Real-time operating systems (RTOS) – provide guaranteed response times in industrial, military, or medical systems (e.g. VxWorks, QNX).
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-12.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Classification of Operating Systems – New Categories

Cloud-oriented operating systems
Foundation for virtual machines and services
Examples: ChromeOS, Azure Sphere, AWS Firecracker
Container-focused operating systems
Minimal systems optimized for running containers
Examples: CoreOS, RancherOS, k3OS
Edge/IoT-specific operating systems
For small, resource-constrained devices
Examples: RIOT OS, Zephyr, TinyOS
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-13.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Operating Systems – The Role of Unix

Adaptable
Unix was originally developed in the 1960s–70s at AT&T Bell Labs.
It was small, portable, and modular → easy to adapt to different hardware.
As a result, it spread rapidly in universities and research environments.

Standard-setting. Unix introduced concepts still used today:
file-system hierarchy (/usr, /bin, etc.),
the “everything is a file” principle (files can represent devices, processes, text),
pipes, processes, and permissions.
Unix formed the basis of the POSIX standard → it still shapes Linux, macOS, and many other operating systems.

A common ancestor. Many modern operating systems descend from Unix or Unix-like systems:
Linux (a Unix-like system in the free/open-source tradition).
BSD systems (FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD; later forming part of the basis of macOS).
Android is also based on the Linux kernel.
This is why Unix is often called a “common ancestor” → its philosophy remains present in many modern operating systems, even when the code is different.
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-14.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Process

A process is a program in execution. It includes the program code, data, and execution state.

Each process has an address space, registers, open files, and resources
The OS records process states in the process table
Scheduling: the OS can suspend and resume a process
Process tree: parent and child processes, cooperation, and IPC (Interprocess Communication)
Signals: handling asynchronous events (e.g. timer, error)
Each process is associated with a user (UID, GID)

Process tree
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-15.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Process States

Possible states:
New – the process is being created.
Ready – the process is ready to run and waiting for CPU time.
Running – the process is currently executing on the CPU.
Waiting / Blocked – the process cannot run because it is waiting for an event (e.g. completion of an I/O operation).
Terminated – the process has finished and the OS releases its resources.

Special states:
Suspended / Stopped – the process is not running but can be resumed.
Zombie – the process has finished, but its parent has not yet collected its status → an entry remains in the process table.
Orphan – the parent has terminated, but the child process continues running
:::

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-17.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Process Control Block

The Process Control Block (PCB) is an OS data structure containing all information required to manage a process.

Contents
Identifiers: PID (Process ID), user ID (UID), group ID (GID)
State: current process state (Running, Ready, Waiting, …)
Registers: saved program counter, stack pointer, and CPU registers
Memory information: address space, page or segment tables
Files and resources: list of open files, I/O connections
Scheduling data: priority, CPU time, quotas

Role
The OS uses PCBs to track and manage processes.
If the scheduler suspends a process, the PCB stores its complete state → execution can later resume exactly where it stopped.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-18.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Threads

A thread is an execution unit within a process.

Threads share the process resources (address space, files).
Each thread has its own program counter, stack, and registers
The operating system provides thread management and scheduling.
Types: kernel threads – managed by the OS; user threads – implemented by libraries rather than directly by the OS
Relationship: process = resources + threads that execute the program.
Threads are lighter-weight than processes (faster context switching).
Concurrency: multiple threads can run within one process (e.g. in a browser, one thread downloads while another renders).
Efficient on multicore processors: threads can execute truly in parallel.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-19.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Address Spaces

An address space is the range of memory a process can use.

It consists of addresses ranging from 0 to a maximum value.
It determines which memory a process can access
Address spaces prevent processes from accessing each other's memory (isolation, protection)
An address space contains:
program code (instructions),
program data (variables, global data),
the stack (function calls, local variables).
Modern applications: sandboxing, virtualization, containers
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-20.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Files

A file is a named unit of data maintained by the operating system for persistent storage and management.

It may contain text, binary data, program code, images, video, etc.
It exists within a namespace (file system, directories).
Files have metadata (size, creation time, permissions).
The OS provides access → read, write, delete, append.

Modern applications:
Files may be network-based (NFS, SMB) or distributed/object-based (HDFS, Amazon S3)
Non-file-system storage also exists (e.g. NoSQL databases, object stores).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-21.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Input/Output

I/O is the OS subsystem that manages input and output devices. It includes device-independent mechanisms and device-specific drivers.

Device-independent I/O
The OS provides general mechanisms that apply to all devices.
Example: abstractions for opening files and reading/writing.
Device-dependent I/O
Handled by device drivers → each hardware device requires a specific driver.
Example: printer or graphics-card driver.

Modern applications: Plug & Play, virtual I/O in cloud VMs
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-22.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Protection

The operating system is responsible for keeping data (e.g. emails, business plans, tax returns) protected and confidential.

Goal: process and data isolation, permission management
User and group identifiers (UID, GID) control access
Superuser / Administrator with special privileges

Modern applications:
With Zero Trust, the OS must continuously verify who is running each process or establishing each network connection and whether access to the resource is authorized
Hardware security (TPM, SGX): the OS provides the appropriate interface
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-23.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Shell

Shell = command interpreter, an interface between the user and the operating system.

A system program that uses OS services.
Its role is to accept and execute commands (launch programs, invoke system calls).
Supports I/O redirection (> and <), pipes (|), and background processes (&)
A GUI serves a similar role → a user interface to the OS.
The shell is often used alongside the GUI

Modern applications:
Automation and scripting (DevOps and cloud workflows)
Managing cloud resources
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-24.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – Kernel

Kernel = the core of the operating system; it directly manages hardware and provides resources to applications.

Main functions (largely the core functions of the operating system)
Process management – creating, scheduling, and terminating processes
Memory management – virtual memory, address spaces, isolation
File system – managing data and metadata
I/O management – device drivers and abstracted hardware access
Protection and permissions – access control
Modern applications:
Monolithic kernel – all functions in one large unit (e.g. Linux)
Microkernel – minimal kernel; many services run in user space (e.g. MINIX, QNX)
Hybrid kernel – combines both approaches (e.g. Windows, macOS XNU)
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-25.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Kernel Types

Monolithic kernel
All major services (process management, memory management, I/O, file system, drivers) are part of the kernel.
Fast → all functions are directly accessible.
Disadvantage: large and complex; faults can affect the whole system.
Microkernel
The kernel contains only essential functions (process management, messaging, minimal memory management); other services (file system, drivers, networking) run as separate user-space processes.
Advantage: modularity, stability, easier debugging. Disadvantage: messaging overhead can reduce performance.
Hybrid kernel
A middle ground: conceptually microkernel-based, but many services run in kernel mode for performance.
Attempts to combine stability and speed.
Nanokernel
An extremely small kernel → mainly interrupt handling and only minimal functionality.
Example: some embedded systems.
Exokernel (experimental approach)
The OS kernel provides direct access to hardware rather than high-level abstractions → applications build their own abstractions.
Highly flexible, but complex for developers. Example: MIT Exokernel project.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-26.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Operating-System Architectures

Classical:
Monolithic system – everything runs in one large kernel (e.g. early UNIX).
Layered system – a well-structured OS divided into layers (e.g. THE system).
Virtual machine – hardware virtualization allowing multiple independent operating systems (e.g. IBM VM/370).
Exokernel – minimal kernel for resource allocation; abstractions implemented in user space (MIT project).
Microkernel – only core functions in the kernel; other services in user space (e.g. MINIX 3, QNX).

Modern:
Hybrid kernel – microkernel principles, but many modules run in kernel mode for performance (e.g. Windows NT, macOS).
Container-based isolation – an OS feature (Linux namespaces, cgroups), used in modern virtualization.
Cloud/distributed OS – managing resources across a cluster or cloud (e.g. Kubernetes as a “cluster OS”).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-27.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – System Calls

A user program cannot access hardware directly; instead, it asks the OS to perform operations through system calls.

Main areas:
process management,
file management,
I/O, 
memory,
communication and protection.
Role
Security: the kernel checks whether the call is authorized.
Abstraction: the program does not need to know hardware details.
Consistent interface: all programs access OS functions in the same way.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-28.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Basic Concepts – User Mode and Kernel Mode

User mode
User programs run in user mode.
Restricted access: programs cannot directly access hardware, memory, or I/O devices.
For privileged operations (e.g. opening files, memory management, networking), the program uses a system call handled by the kernel.
Goal: protection → faulty or malicious programs cannot crash the entire system.
Kernel mode (supervisor / privileged mode)
The kernel and device drivers run here.
Full access to hardware, memory, and CPU instructions.
This is where the core of the operating system runs.
When control enters kernel mode, the OS has full privileges.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-29.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – Windows 11 Architecture

Hybrid kernel
Neither purely microkernel nor purely monolithic.
Originally based on microkernel principles (NT design), but many components remained in kernel mode for performance → hence the hybrid design.
Main characteristics
Kernel mode: NT kernel, device drivers, memory management, scheduler.
User mode: Win32 subsystem, UWP, former POSIX compatibility, .NET CLR.
Subsystems: Windows provides multiple APIs for compatibility.
Security model: ACLs, UAC, sandboxing, and mandatory TPM 2.0 hardware support in Windows 11.
Examples of architecture layers
User space: graphical interface (Explorer, UWP apps), system programs.
Kernel space: hybrid NT kernel, HAL (Hardware Abstraction Layer), drivers.
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-30.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – Linux Architecture

Characteristics
Monolithic kernel, but dynamically extensible through kernel modules.
User space and kernel space are clearly separated.
Device drivers and file systems are part of the kernel and can be loaded as modules.
Hardware abstraction (device drivers, architecture-specific code).
Supports containers (namespaces, cgroups) and virtual machines (KVM).
:::


---

## {background-image="../slides/lecture-03/slide-31.png" background-size="100% 100%" background-position="center" background-repeat="no-repeat"}

::: {.notes}
Example – macOS Architecture

Characteristics
UNIX-based (POSIX-compatible, built partly on BSD).
Hybrid kernel: XNU (X is Not Unix).
Microkernel elements: Mach (process management, IPC, memory).
Monolithic elements: BSD (file system, networking, security).
I/O Kit: object-oriented driver model.
:::
